analysis: Examined three changes. (1) LaunchAgent.swift (head 282-302): the daemon env allowlist gains PromptTokenCachePolicy (enable/capacity/verify), ChatTemplateLoopRewrites and WorkFIFOPolicy.coldLoadReleaseEnvironmentKey. Only non-empty allowlisted values are copied from the installing shell into the plist, so there is no arbitrary env injection. The local operator is already the adversary (TB-003) and these are rollback or tuning knobs. The plist keys and the stop/disable lifecycle are unchanged. (2) JinjaSanitization.swift (head 71-79): a fast path returns exact String/Int/Double/Bool/NSNumber/NSString leaves before Mirror reflection. Boxed Optionals have type Optional<...>, so they miss the fast path and are still unwrapped. NSNull and the JSONNull struct do not match the leaf types. The earlier checks returned these leaves verbatim, so output is unchanged, with no sanitization bypass and no consumer-visible behavior change. (3) BenchmarkCommand.swift (head 193-202, 305-320, 440): a new --prompt-prep CLI mode. It is mutually exclusive with other modes, takes only synthetic prompts, and loads only the tokenizer. No network, key or attestation surface. Length parsing filters to positive Ints, though huge values could cause local resource exhaustion only for the operator who runs the command. Open integration question: LaunchAgent's comments describe a new on-by-default scoped prompt-token cache (PromptTokenCachePolicy). Its implementation is not in the supplied evidence. If it reuses tokenization or prompt state across consumers, it could add a cross-tenant timing or retention channel beyond T-041/SEC-035 (A-001). Reviewers must confirm that its scope key is coordinator-authored (account/model/prompt-contract), that it is memory-only with TTL and bounds, that it never persists plaintext, and that the threat model records it. This cannot be concluded from these files, so I flag deeper review rather than a finding.
